title: The Makkah Pact Is Bridging the Gulf and South Asia
author: Saima Afzal
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/artur-voznenko-
KGxOqAiOhX0-unsplash-1-680x452.jpg)

Image by Artur Voznenko.

The [Makkah Joint Defence Agreement](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-
pacific/saudi-arabia-turkey-pakistan-sign-joint-defence-deal-amid-regional-
turmoil-2026-08-07/), signed by Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye on August
7, has quickly invited comparisons with an “Islamic NATO.” Initially, that
analogy appeared premature. But subsequent statements by senior Pakistani and
Turkish officials have made it harder to dismiss altogether.

Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Asif has [advocated a
NATO](https://blogs.timesofisrael.com/pakistan-wants-to-turn-the-mecca-pact-
into-an-islamic-anti-israel-nato/)-like collective-defence arrangement among
Muslim countries. Turkish Foreign Minister [Hakan
Fidan](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GO7Q7Z6F_CY) has gone further,
describing the Makkah agreement as technically comparable to NATO’s Article 5
and discussing plans for a ministerial mechanism and permanent secretariat in
Saudi Arabia.

Riyadh has been more circumspect, avoiding an official characterisation of the
pact as another NATO. This difference matters. While the three governments
broadly agree on strengthening collective deterrence, they may not yet attach
identical political or institutional meaning to the arrangement.

The NATO analogy is therefore revealing but premature. NATO’s credibility
rests not simply on its [collective-
defence](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/dispatches/why-saudi-arabia-pakistan-
and-turkey-just-signed-a-defense-pact/) clause but on decades of integrated
military planning, command structures, interoperability, intelligence
coordination and political consultation. The Makkah pact has yet to
demonstrate anything comparable.

Its significance lies elsewhere. The accord begins to [connect Gulf and South
Asian](https://www.facebook.com/INSS.IL/posts/saudi-arabia-and-pakistan-an-
end-to-ambiguitydr-yoel-guzansky-a-senior-researche/1231429079028937/)
security within a common framework, as regional powers seek additional
mechanisms for managing uncertainty without abandoning established external
partnerships.

**Saudi Arabia’s Search for Security Insurance**

For Saudi Arabia, the accord reflects a reassessment of security in an
increasingly volatile region.

[Riyadh](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/7/turkiye-saudi-arabi-pakistan-
sign-joint-defence-agreement-whats-in-it) has traditionally depended heavily
on the United States for deterrence and advanced military capabilities. But
attacks on Gulf infrastructure, threats to energy routes and successive
regional crises have exposed the risks of relying overwhelmingly on one
external security provider.

The conclusion is not that Washington has become irrelevant. Saudi Arabia
remains deeply connected to the United States through defence, economic and
strategic ties. Riyadh instead appears determined to supplement that
relationship with additional partnerships.

By bringing Turkiye and Pakistan into a [collective-defence
framework](https://www.tbsnews.net/explainer/what-mecca-joint-deterrence-
agreement-between-turkiye-saudi-arabia-and-pakistan-1509391), Saudi Arabia
broadens the range of actors a potential aggressor must consider. The
agreement does not publicly specify a predetermined military response, but
that uncertainty may itself contribute to deterrence: aggression could
generate wider political, logistical or military consequences.

**What Turkiye and Pakistan Bring**

Türkiye broadens the framework beyond the longstanding Saudi-Pakistani defence
relationship.

Ankara combines a large conventional military and
[NATO](https://cnaws.in/situational-reports/saudi-arabia-turkey-and-pakistan-
mutual-defence-pact-what-the-mecca-agreement-means-for-west-asia-and-india/)
experience with a rapidly expanding defence industry. Its capabilities
complement Saudi efforts to strengthen domestic defence production and
diversify procurement. Joint production, technology partnerships, exercises
and greater interoperability could eventually prove more consequential than
the pact’s headline collective-defence provision.

For Ankara, the pact also offers greater strategic reach. Turkiye is not
replacing NATO with a regional bloc; it is adding another partnership to a
foreign policy increasingly characterised by overlapping relationships.

Pakistan brings different assets. Decades of [military
cooperation](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/08/09/pakistan-says-new-
defense-pact-with-saudi-arabia-and-turkey-is-purely-defensive-01030194) with
Saudi Arabia, substantial manpower and operational experience make Islamabad a
natural security partner. Pakistan’s nuclear status adds to its broader
strategic weight, although the agreement provides no basis for assuming that
Islamabad has extended a nuclear umbrella to Saudi Arabia.

Pakistan’s [diplomatic
position](https://en.majalla.com/node/332387/politics/pakistan%E2%80%99s-red-
sea-calculus-and-end-strategic-ambiguity) is equally significant. Islamabad
has sought workable relations with competing regional actors and positioned
itself as a potential intermediary during periods of tension. [Pakistan’s
participation](https://www.irananalytica.org/p/how-iran-sees-the-mecca-
defense-pact) therefore complicates attempts to portray the pact as an
explicitly anti-Iran coalition. Islamabad shares a border with Iran and has
strong strategic incentives to preserve stable relations with Tehran.

The interests of the three members are complementary without being identical.
That may prove both the pact’s strength and its principal challenge.

**Iran and Ambiguous Deterrence**

Iran remains an important strategic variable despite not being named in the
agreement. Iran’s missile and drone capabilities, Iran-aligned armed groups,
[Houthi operations](https://gulfnews.com/world/gulf/saudi/hormuz-shut-red-sea-
under-threat-saudi-arabia-faces-a-new-houthi-front-1.500635331) and threats to
maritime routes have become important factors in Gulf threat perceptions. For
Saudi Arabia, strengthening deterrence amid such risks is understandable.

Yet none of the three signatories has an interest in institutionalising
permanent confrontation with Tehran. Turkiye combines strategic competition
with economic and diplomatic engagement. Pakistan has strong incentives to
maintain stability along its Iranian border. Saudi Arabia also has reasons to
prevent regional instability from undermining its economic transformation.

The accord therefore attempts something more subtle than constructing an anti-
Iran bloc. It seeks to raise the potential costs of aggression without
formally identifying where that aggression might originate.

This preserves diplomatic space while allowing the agreement to address a
broader range of threats. But strategic ambiguity works only if potential
adversaries believe the collective-defence commitment carries consequences.

**The Non-State Actor Problem**

That becomes more complicated when aggression does not come directly from
another state.

The Middle East’s security environment is shaped by drones, missiles, militias
and proxy networks as much as conventional warfare. Would a major Houthi
missile or drone attack on Saudi territory activate the agreement? Would
Turkiye and Pakistan respond militarily, provide intelligence or air-defence
assistance, or offer diplomatic support?

Similar questions arise beyond the Gulf. If another India-Pakistan
confrontation escalated, how would [Riyadh and
Ankara](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CVdgsAt8unU) interpret the scope of
their commitments to Islamabad? Turkiye’s NATO membership adds another layer
of complexity.

These questions go directly to deterrence. Collective defence becomes credible
when adversaries believe an attack will impose costs, but members also need
sufficient flexibility to prevent a local confrontation from producing
uncontrolled escalation.

The pact’s credibility will therefore depend on institution-building. A
permanent secretariat and ministerial mechanism could provide political
coordination, but military credibility would require intelligence sharing,
joint exercises, contingency planning, logistical arrangements and agreed
consultation procedures.

Without such mechanisms, the pact will remain primarily a political signal.
With them, it could evolve into a meaningful security institution without
becoming a NATO-style alliance.

**Bridging the Gulf and South Asia**

Perhaps the pact’s most consequential feature is that it begins to
institutionalise a strategic bridge between two security theatres
traditionally treated as distinct.

Pakistan’s participation means a [collective-defence
framework](https://cnaws.in/situational-reports/saudi-arabia-turkey-and-
pakistan-mutual-defence-pact-what-the-mecca-agreement-means-for-west-asia-and-
india/) centred partly on Gulf security now reaches into an environment shaped
by India-Pakistan rivalry, China’s regional role and nuclear deterrence.

The connection works in the opposite direction. Gulf instability has direct
implications for Pakistan through energy security, investment, military
cooperation and relations with Iran.

This does not mean Saudi Arabia or Türkiye will automatically become parties
to South Asian conflicts, or that Pakistan will participate in every Gulf
confrontation. The absence of such automaticity may be precisely what allows
the arrangement to function.

The pact’s significance is therefore not simply that Pakistan has joined
another defence arrangement. It potentially changes the geography through
which regional security is understood, bringing Gulf deterrence and South
Asian strategic competition into closer interaction.

**Beyond Reliance on Washington**

For decades, much of the Middle East’s security architecture revolved around
external guarantees, particularly those provided by the United States. The
Makkah pact suggests that regional states increasingly want arrangements they
can shape themselves alongside established partnerships.

This is neither necessarily an American retreat nor a rejection of Washington.
The United States retains military capabilities, intelligence networks and
logistical reach that Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan cannot collectively
reproduce.

What is changing is exclusivity. Saudi Arabia can retain its American security
relationship while deepening defence cooperation with Türkiye and Pakistan.
Türkiye can remain in NATO while developing additional regional frameworks.
Pakistan can sustain its strategic partnership with China while maintaining
relationships with Washington, Riyadh, Ankara and Tehran.

For Washington, greater regional capacity could support burden-sharing. But
greater responsibility will also bring greater autonomy, including initiatives
the United States does not exclusively design or control.

**The Real Test of Makkah**

The central question is whether Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan can turn a
political commitment to collective defence into credible security cooperation.

The three bring distinct assets: Saudi economic and political weight, Turkish
military and defence-industrial capabilities, and Pakistani military
experience and diplomatic reach. But collective defence is easier to declare
than to implement.

The pact must establish how members consult during crises, distinguish state
aggression from attacks by non-state actors, and determine what assistance
each is prepared to provide. Its durability will also depend on whether the
governments can manage relationships outside the pact, particularly with Iran.

If effective consultation, military coordination and crisis-management
mechanisms develop, Makkah could become an early institutional expression of a
more diversified regional security order. The growing use of NATO terminology
by Pakistani and Turkish officials signals political ambition; whether that
rhetoric acquires operational meaning will depend on the institutions built
around it.

The pact’s larger significance lies in bringing Gulf and South Asian security
into closer interaction while reflecting a wider shift towards regional agency
and overlapping partnerships.

Its ultimate test will not be whether its leaders compare it with NATO, but
whether it can make aggression more costly without making escalation more
likely.
